I10.overview: A condition characterised by elevated blood pressure measured on 3 separate occasions, a minimum of 2 days apart: systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg.
phases: Step 1 — Lifestyle modification (3 months trial if no risk factors)
Step 2 — Add thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic
Step 3 — Add second antihypertensive
Step 4 — Increase dose of second medicine
Step 5 — Add third antihypertensive
Step 6 — Increase dose of third medicine
Step 7 — Add fourth medicine (spironolactone) — refer if uncontrolled

medications.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
medications.notes: Thiazide diuretic. Contraindicated in gout, pregnancy, severe liver impairment, eGFR < 30 mL/min.

medications.name: Amlodipine
medications.notes: Long-acting calcium channel blocker. Avoid in untreated heart failure.

medications.name: Enalapril
medications.notes: ACE-inhibitor. Contraindicated in pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, aortic valve stenosis, history of angioedema, hyperkalaemia, eGFR < 30 mL/min.

medications.name: Spironolactone
medications.notes: Doctor-initiated only. Risk of severe hyperkalaemia — monitor serum potassium within 1 month of therapy and thereafter. Do NOT use with potassium supplements or NSAIDs.

lifestyleAdvice: Stop smoking
Maintain ideal weight (BMI 18–25 kg/m²)
Salt restriction — remove salt from table, reduce salt in cooking, avoid processed foods
Increase potassium intake from fresh fruits and vegetables
Reduce alcohol to ≤ 2 standard drinks/day for males, ≤ 1 for females
Follow a healthy eating plan (low fat, high fibre, unrefined carbohydrates)
Regular moderate aerobic exercise — 30 minutes brisk walking, 5–7 times/week

baseline: Serum potassium (if on ACE-inhibitor or eGFR < 30 mL/min)
sixMonthly: Serum potassium (if on spironolactone or eGFR < 30 mL/min)

I10.followUpSchedule: Monthly monitoring and therapy adjustment until BP is stable. Once target BP achieved, review every 3–6 months. If lifestyle modification alone, re-assess after 3 months.
warningSigns: Severe headache with blurred vision or confusion
Chest pain / unstable angina
Shortness of breath / pulmonary oedema
Neurological signs — coma, seizures, visual disturbances
Signs of renal failure
referralCriteria: BP not controlled on 4 medicines and no doctor available

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Systolic BP > 180 mmHg and/or diastolic BP > 130 mmHg WITH organ damage symptoms
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Amlodipine 10 mg oral as single dose. If pulmonary oedema: Furosemide 40 mg IV.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening — needs immediate referral to hospital

specialCases.note: Initiate medicine treatment only when BP > 160/90 mmHg. Lower BP slowly over a few days.
See Section 6.4.2 — Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Do NOT treat elevated BP at PHC — refer urgently

I10.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 4, Section 4.7.1

E11.9.overview: A chronic metabolic disease characterised by hyperglycaemia with serious acute and chronic complications. Most adults with type 2 diabetes are overweight.

glycaemicTargets.patientType: Young, low risk / Newly diagnosed / No CVD

phases: Step 1 — Lifestyle modification + Metformin
Step 2 — Add sulphonylurea (if HbA1c not at target after 2–3 months)
Step 3 — Insulin therapy (doctor-initiated; stop sulphonylurea, continue metformin)

medications.name: Metformin
medications.frequency: Once daily with meals, titrate slowly
medications.notes: First-line agent. Contraindicated in uncontrolled congestive cardiac failure, severe liver disease, significant respiratory compromise, and renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min).

medications.name: Gliclazide
medications.notes: Preferred sulphonylurea in the elderly. Only add if HbA1c > 8% despite 2–3 months of maximal metformin. Missing meals may cause hypoglycaemia.

medications.name: Insulin (Intermediate to long-acting)
medications.notes: Doctor-initiated. If 10 units ineffective, increase gradually to 20 units (2–4 unit increase per week). Continue metformin; STOP sulphonylurea when insulin is initiated.

lifestyleAdvice: Regular, evenly-spaced meals with small portions
Nutritionally balanced meals — one protein, one starch, two vegetables, one fruit, water
Strict carbohydrate control — favour whole grains, legumes, vegetables
Discourage processed/refined carbs (takeaways, cakes, white bread, sugary drinks)
Aim for 5 servings of fruit/vegetables per day; limit fruit to 2 servings/day
Prefer fat-free or low-fat dairy
Eat oily fish (sardines, pilchards) 2–3 times per week
Salt: do not exceed half a teaspoon per day
Increased physical activity — 30 minutes, 5 times a week
Appropriate weight loss if overweight
Stop smoking; limit alcohol
Foot care education — inspect feet daily
Wear a medical notification bracelet

portionGuide.protein: Size of your palm (about 90 g or ½ cup)
portionGuide.fruitsVegStarch: No larger than your clenched fist (1 cup)

E11.9.followUpSchedule: Review monthly until stable. Once at target, review every 3–6 months. HbA1c every 3–6 months while therapy changes. Annual comprehensive review.
warningSigns: Blood glucose < 4 mmol/L (hypoglycaemia) — treat immediately
Altered level of consciousness
Acidotic breathing (DKA)
Dehydration and hypotension
Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain
Ketonuria (more than 1+)
Hyperglycaemia > 25 mmol/L
Sudden deterioration of vision
Serious infections

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Altered level of consciousness, acidotic breathing, dehydration, ketonuria, or glucose > 25 mmol/L
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Check blood glucose and test urine for ketones. If diagnosis uncertain, treat as hypoglycaemia and refer urgently.

hypoglycaemiaTreatment.conscious: Sweets, sugar, glucose by mouth, OR oral sugar solution (3 tsp sugar in 200 mL water)
hypoglycaemiaTreatment.unconscious: Dextrose 10% IV, 2–5 mL/kg. Re-check glucose 10–15 min later.

E11.9.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 9, Section 9.2.2

B20.overview: HIV is a retrovirus that attacks the immune system, specifically CD4 lymphocytes. Without treatment it progressively destroys immunity, leading to opportunistic infections and AIDS. With effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), people living with HIV can achieve near-normal life expectancy. All PLHIV are eligible for ART, regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage.
phases: Diagnosis — confirm with 2 rapid tests from different manufacturers; do CD4 count and WHO staging
ART initiation — start TLD as soon as feasible, ideally same-day if patient is ready
Monitoring — VL at 3 & 10 months, then annually if suppressed
Long-term care — continued adherence support and viral suppression

medications.name: Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (TLD)
medications.dosage: TDF 300 mg + 3TC 300 mg + DTG 50 mg (single tablet)
medications.phase: First-line ART — Treatment-naïve patients ≥30 kg and ≥10 years
medications.notes: The preferred first-line regimen for all adults including women of child-bearing potential. Check creatinine before starting TDF — avoid TDF if eGFR <50 mL/min. If HBsAg positive, TDF must form part of the regimen.

medications.name: TDF + Emtricitabine + Efavirenz (TEE)
medications.dosage: TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg + EFV 600 mg
medications.phase: Alternative first-line — patients on rifampicin-based TB treatment who cannot use DTG
medications.notes: Used when patient is on rifampicin-based TB treatment and cannot double-dose DTG, or has DTG intolerance/contraindication.

medications.name: TDF + 3TC + DTG (with double-dose DTG)
medications.dosage: TDF 300 mg + 3TC 300 mg + DTG 50 mg twice daily
medications.duration: During TB treatment + 2 weeks after stopping rifampicin
medications.phase: Alternative — patients on rifampicin-based TB treatment
medications.notes: Rifampicin reduces DTG concentrations. Additional 50 mg DTG dose given 12 hours after the TLD dose. Stop the extra DTG dose 2 weeks after stopping rifampicin.

medications.name: TDF + 3TC/FTC + Atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r)
medications.phase: Protease inhibitor-based regimen — contraindications to BOTH EFV and DTG
medications.notes: If patient requires rifampicin-based TB treatment, substitute ATV/r with LPV/r at 800/200 mg 12-hourly. Avoid co-administration with proton-pump inhibitors.

medications.name: Abacavir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (ALD)
medications.phase: Alternative — TDF contraindication (eGFR <50 mL/min), no chronic hepatitis B
medications.notes: If chronic hepatitis B coinfection AND eGFR 30-50 mL/min, use TAF + FTC + DTG instead. ABC can cause hypersensitivity reactions — if suspected, consult expert.

medications.name: Zidovudine + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir
medications.dosage: AZT 300 mg + 3TC 150 mg (twice daily) + DTG 50 mg daily
medications.frequency: AZT/3TC twice daily; DTG once daily
medications.phase: Alternative — intolerance to TDF/TAF and ABC
medications.notes: Monitor FBC at months 1 and 3 for AZT-related anaemia. AZT dose adjusted in renal impairment.

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole (OI prophylaxis)
medications.notes: Indicated for WHO stage 3/4 or CD4 <200. Stop when CD4 >200. Watch for maculopapular rash — stop and refer if systemic features or mucosal involvement.

medications.name: Isoniazid (TB Preventive Therapy)
medications.phase: TB Preventive Therapy (TPT) — additional to ART
medications.notes: Give to all adult PLHIV who don't have active TB, liver disease, or prior MDR/XDR-TB. Exclude TB first. Add pyridoxine 25 mg daily. Follow up monthly for first 3 months. Educate on hepatotoxicity symptoms. Defer in pregnancy until after delivery.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

lifestyleAdvice: Take your ART at the same time every day — adherence is essential for viral suppression
Never skip doses — resistance develops quickly from missed doses
Use condoms during sexual intercourse to prevent transmission and STIs
Disclose your HIV status to someone who can be your treatment supporter
Join a support or peer group for people living with HIV
Seek early treatment for any sexually transmitted infection
Inform all sexual partners so they can be tested and treated
Eat a balanced diet and maintain a healthy weight
Exercise regularly to support immune function
Stop smoking and limit alcohol — both weaken the immune system
Get your flu vaccine annually
Attend every clinic appointment — do not run out of medication
If you have TB symptoms (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss), report them immediately

baseline: If CD4 <200: cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test — do LP if positive
Screen for pregnancy (or ask if planning to conceive)
Screen for mental health, STIs, and non-communicable diseases
Screen for TB using WHO questionnaire (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss)
Urine LAM for inpatients or outpatients with CD4 <200 / advanced HIV
If planning TDF: serum creatinine (avoid TDF if eGFR <50 mL/min)
HBsAg (if positive, TDF must form part of regimen)
onART: Viral load at 3 and 10 months after ART initiation, then every 12 months if virologically suppressed
CD4 at 10 months; stop once CD4 >200 AND virologically suppressed
If on TDF: creatinine at month 3, month 10, then annually
If on AZT: FBC and differential at 1 and 3 months
If on protease inhibitor: cholesterol and triglycerides at month 3
ALT if symptoms of hepatitis develop
Weight, blood pressure, adherence check at every visit

B20.followUpSchedule: Viral load at 3 and 10 months after ART initiation and every 12 months thereafter if virologically suppressed. Clinical review at every script refill.
warningSigns: New or worsening cough lasting more than 2 weeks (possible TB)
Fever with night sweats and weight loss
Severe headache with neck stiffness (possible meningitis)
Difficulty swallowing or painful swallowing (possible oesophageal candidiasis)
Blurred vision or sudden vision changes
Confusion, seizures, or altered level of consciousness
Severe diarrhoea lasting more than 2 weeks
Shortness of breath at rest
New skin lesions, especially purple or dark patches (possible Kaposi's sarcoma)
Persistent mouth sores or oral thrush not responding to treatment
referralCriteria: Dolutegravir resistance demonstrated on resistance testing
Cryptococcal meningitis (defer ART for 4-6 weeks after starting antifungals)
Virological failure on TLD >2 years with 2 consecutive VL ≥1000 copies/mL
Renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min) requiring specialist care
Chronic hepatitis B coinfection on TDF — do not stop TDF without specialist advice
Severe adverse drug reactions (e.g. abacavir hypersensitivity, AZT-related severe anaemia)

emergencyProtocol.trigger: New severe symptoms in an HIV+ patient — especially fever + neck stiffness, altered consciousness, or severe dyspnoea
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Assess ABCDE. If signs of meningitis (fever + neck stiffness + headache): refer urgently for LP and CSF CrAg. If suspected IRIS: assess severity, do not stop ART, refer to infectious disease specialist.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Most HIV-related emergencies need hospital referral. Do not delay transfer.

specialCases.note: Initiate ART immediately with TLD if no contraindication. See Section 6.8 for pregnancy-specific ART.
Start TB treatment first. Add ART based on CD4: <50 = start within 2 weeks; ≥50 = defer until 8 weeks. Watch for IRIS.
Defer ART for 8 weeks after starting TB treatment regardless of CD4 count. Earlier initiation increases risk of death from IRIS.
Defer ART for 4-6 weeks after starting antifungal therapy. Earlier initiation increases mortality.
Start ART immediately — no delay needed. Treat cryptococcosis with fluconazole as per protocol.
TDF must form part of the ART regimen. Do not stop TDF without specialist advice — risk of fatal hepatitis flare.

specialCases.case: Patient not ready to start ART immediately
specialCases.note: Counsel about benefits and risks. Repeat CD4 count every 6 months until ART can be initiated.
Polyvalent cations (antacids, iron, calcium, zinc) — take DTG 6 hours before or 2 hours after. Metformin — monitor renal function. Carbamazepine/phenytoin/phenobarbital — avoid or double DTG dose.

B20.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 11, Section 11.1 (Antiretroviral therapy, adults and adolescents)

Z21.overview: A patient who has tested HIV-positive but has no current symptoms of HIV disease (WHO clinical stage 1). Despite being asymptomatic, ART should be initiated as soon as feasible — early treatment prevents disease progression, reduces transmission, and improves long-term outcomes. All PLHIV are eligible for ART regardless of CD4 count.
phases: Confirm HIV-positive status — do CD4 count and baseline investigations
Start ART as soon as feasible — same-day initiation if patient is ready
Monitor viral load — target undetectable (<50 copies/mL)
Lifelong adherence support

medications.name: Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (TLD)
medications.notes: Same first-line regimen as for symptomatic HIV. Preferred for all adults including women of child-bearing potential.

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole (prophylaxis — if indicated)
medications.notes: Only if CD4 <200 cells/mm³ or WHO stage 3/4. Asymptomatic patients with CD4 >200 do not require this.

lifestyleAdvice: Take your ART every day at the same time — even when you feel healthy
Use condoms during sexual intercourse to prevent transmission and STIs
Inform your sexual partners so they can be tested
Disclose your status to a trusted person for support
Attend every clinic appointment — do not miss doses or script refills
Maintain a healthy lifestyle — balanced diet, regular exercise, no smoking
Avoid alcohol excess — it affects adherence and liver health
Get your annual flu vaccine
Report any new symptoms to your CHW or clinic promptly
Join a support group for people living with HIV

baseline: Confirm HIV-positive status with 2 rapid tests (different manufacturers)
Screen for TB (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss)
Screen for mental health, STIs, NCDs
onART: Viral load at 3 and 10 months, then annually if suppressed
CD4 at 10 months (stop if >200 and suppressed)
Creatinine (if on TDF) at month 3, month 10, then annually
Weight, blood pressure, adherence check at every visit

Z21.followUpSchedule: Same as for symptomatic HIV — VL at 3 and 10 months after ART initiation, then annually if suppressed. Clinical review at each script refill.
warningSigns: Any new symptom that could indicate HIV progression — weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, persistent fever
New cough lasting >2 weeks (possible TB)
Oral thrush or difficulty swallowing
Skin rash or lesions
Swollen glands lasting more than a few weeks
referralCriteria: Any new symptoms suggesting WHO stage 2, 3, or 4 progression
Pregnancy planning (refer for preconception ART review)
Z21.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 11, Section 11.1 (Antiretroviral therapy, adults and adolescents)

Z29.2.conditionName: HIV prophylaxis (cotrimoxazole and TB preventive therapy)
Z29.2.overview: Preventive treatment for people living with HIV to reduce the risk of opportunistic infections. Includes cotrimoxazole prophylaxis (against Pneumocystis pneumonia, toxoplasmosis, and bacterial infections) and TB Preventive Therapy (TPT) with isoniazid. Both are given alongside ART for eligible patients.
Z29.2.treatmentDurationText: Varies — cotrimoxazole until CD4 >200; TPT for 12 months
phases: Initiation — after excluding active infections
Maintenance — continued prophylaxis
Discontinuation — when criteria met

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole
medications.notes: Indicated for WHO Clinical stage 3 or 4, or CD4 <200 cells/mm³. Once CD4 >200, discontinue. If CD4 was >200 when commenced (e.g. TB), continue for 6 months. Watch for maculopapular rash — stop immediately and refer if systemic features or mucosal involvement occur.

medications.name: Isoniazid (INH)
medications.notes: Give to all adult PLHIV at any CD4 count and any ART status. Exclude active TB first. Exclusions: suspected/confirmed TB, liver disease, prior MDR/XDR-TB, painful peripheral neuropathy, alcohol use disorder. For patients on a DTG-based ART regimen, isoniazid daily for 12 months is preferred.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy. Counsel patient to report any tingling or numbness.

lifestyleAdvice: Take your prophylaxis every day at the same time as your ART
Do not stop cotrimoxazole or isoniazid without telling your clinic
Report any new rash, tingling in hands/feet, or yellow eyes to your CHW immediately
If you have any TB symptoms (cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss), report them before starting TPT
Continue all your HIV care — prophylaxis is additional, not a replacement
Attend monthly check-ups for the first 3 months of TPT

everyVisit: Ask about tingling or numbness in hands/feet (isoniazid neuropathy)
Ask about nausea, vomiting, yellow eyes, brown urine, RUQ pain (isoniazid hepatotoxicity)
baseline: Exclude active TB before starting TPT

Z29.2.followUpSchedule: Cotrimoxazole: continue until CD4 >200; review at each ART visit. TPT: monthly follow-up for first 3 months, then routine; complete the full 12-month course.
warningSigns: New rash — especially with fever, mucosal involvement, or facial swelling (cotrimoxazole hypersensitivity)
Tingling or numbness in hands or feet (isoniazid neuropathy)
Nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite (isoniazid hepatotoxicity)
Yellow eyes or skin (jaundice)
Dark brown urine
Pain in the right upper abdomen (liver)
Any TB symptom appearing while on prophylaxis
referralCriteria: Severe cotrimoxazole hypersensitivity (rash with systemic features or mucosal involvement)

specialCases.note: Defer TPT until after delivery. Continue routine TB screening at every antenatal visit.
Do NOT use rifapentine-containing 3HP regimen. Use daily isoniazid for 12 months.
Do NOT use rifapentine-containing 3HP regimen — reduces contraceptive efficacy.
Exclude from TPT. Continue routine TB screening.

Z29.2.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 11, Sections 11.2.1 and 11.2.2

A15.overview: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, most commonly affecting the lungs. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. TB is a notifiable disease. Drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB) is treated with a 6-month regimen: 2 months of intensive-phase RHZE followed by 4 months of continuation-phase RH. Cure rates are high with correct, complete treatment.
phases: Intensive phase (Months 1–2) — RHZE 4-drug combination daily
Continuation phase (Months 3–6) — RH 2-drug combination daily
Cure — sputum smear-negative at month 5 or 6

medications.name: RHZE — Rifampicin + Isoniazid + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (fixed-dose combination)
medications.frequency: Once daily, same time each day
medications.notes: The 4-in-1 tablet contains Rifampicin 150 mg + Isoniazid 75 mg + Pyrazinamide 400 mg + Ethambutol 275 mg. Take all tablets in ONE dose (not divided). Tablets may be taken with food to minimise nausea. Rifampicin may turn urine, sweat and tears orange — this is harmless. Rifampicin reduces the effectiveness of combined oral contraceptives and progestin-only implants — advise alternative contraception (IUD, DMPA) or additional barrier method.

medications.name: RH — Rifampicin + Isoniazid (fixed-dose combination)
medications.frequency: Once daily, same time each day
medications.notes: Two formulations available: RH 150/75 mg and RH 300/150 mg. Depending on weight, either 5 tablets of RH 150/75 OR 2 tablets of RH 300/150 is used. Continue taking treatment every day without interruption.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.duration: Full duration of TB treatment (6 months)
medications.phase: Adjunct — given with all TB medicines
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy. Given routinely to patients with HIV, malnutrition, or existing neuropathy.

lifestyleAdvice: Take all your TB tablets every day without missing any dose — this is essential for cure
Take all tablets together in ONE dose at the same time each day
You may take tablets with food to reduce nausea
Do not stop treatment even if you feel better — completing 6 months is essential to prevent resistance
If you miss more than 2 doses, tell your CHW or clinic immediately
Cover your mouth when you cough or sneeze — TB spreads through the air
Open windows and let in sunlight at home — TB spreads less in well-ventilated spaces
Sleep in a separate room from others if possible during the first 2 weeks of treatment
Eat a nutritious, balanced diet — TB treatment works best with good nutrition
Stop smoking and avoid excessive alcohol — both worsen TB and slow recovery
Attend every follow-up appointment, including sputum tests at 2, 5 and 6 months
Wear a mask in crowded public spaces while you are still infectious (first 2 weeks)
Inform close contacts (family, colleagues) so they can be screened for TB
If you have HIV, take your ART alongside TB treatment every day
Report any of these immediately: yellow eyes/skin, dark urine, severe nausea, tingling in hands/feet, skin rash

everyVisit: Weight — adjust tablet count if weight changes significantly
Ask about adherence — how many doses missed
Ask about side effects (nausea, rash, tingling, yellow eyes)
Check for new symptoms suggesting treatment failure (persistent cough, fever, weight loss)
baseline: Sputum TB-NAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra) — confirm TB and check for rifampicin resistance
HIV test — if positive, refer for ART
Baseline ALT (if jaundiced or risk factors for liver disease)
atMonths: Month 2 — sputum smear microscopy (should convert to negative)
Month 5 — sputum smear microscopy (should remain negative)

A15.followUpSchedule: Monthly clinical review. Sputum smear microscopy at month 2, month 5, and month 6. If smear remains positive at month 2, consider adherence issues and drug-resistant TB — refer for evaluation. If positive at month 5 or 6, refer for investigation of treatment failure.
warningSigns: Yellow eyes or skin (jaundice)
Dark brown urine
Severe nausea or vomiting with abdominal pain
New skin rash — especially with fever, mucosal involvement, or facial swelling
Tingling or numbness in hands or feet
Persistent fever or worsening cough after starting treatment
Coughing up blood (haemoptysis)
Severe chest pain or difficulty breathing
Weight loss despite treatment
referralCriteria: TB meningitis (refer urgently — defer ART for 8 weeks)
Drug-resistant TB confirmed or suspected (Rifampicin-resistant, MDR, XDR)
Failure to convert to smear-negative at month 2 despite adherence
Treatment failure (positive smear at month 5 or 6)
Severe adverse drug reactions (hepatitis, drug rash, peripheral neuropathy worsening despite pyridoxine)
TB in children (<12 years) requiring chest X-ray for diagnosis
Contact of a patient with drug-resistant TB
Unable to be managed on an ambulatory basis (e.g. severe clinical condition)
Pregnancy — refer for expert TB management

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Signs of disseminated TB, TB meningitis, or severe adverse drug reaction (hepatitis, drug rash with systemic features)
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Refer to hospital same day. For suspected TB meningitis (fever + neck stiffness + headache): urgent LP and referral. For suspected drug-induced hepatitis: STOP all TB medicines before referral.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening if not treated promptly. Do not delay referral.

specialCases.note: Treat TB and HIV. Start TB treatment first, then add ART based on CD4: <50 = within 2 weeks; ≥50 = defer until 8 weeks. Watch for Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS). Rifampicin reduces DTG concentration — double DTG dose to 50 mg twice daily while on rifampicin (extra dose 12 hours after TLD).
Ethambutol 15–25 mg/kg three times weekly. Pyrazinamide 20–30 mg/kg three times weekly. Rifampicin and isoniazid do not require dose adjustment.
Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol are all safe in pregnancy. Do NOT use pyridoxine-free regimen — give pyridoxine 25 mg daily. Refer to Section 6.4.2 for obstetric management.
Rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide can cause hepatitis. If jaundice or hepatitis symptoms develop: stop all TB medicines, refer urgently for same-day ALT, do not restart until specialist advice.

Give 25 mg daily alongside TB treatment to prevent isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy — especially important for patients living with HIV, pregnant women, malnourished patients, and those with existing neuropathy.
Where possible, all TB patients should have a treatment supporter (family member, CHW, or clinic staff) to observe each dose and support adherence. Missed doses must be followed up the same day.

Rifampicin reduces the efficacy of combined oral contraceptives and progestin-only implants. Advise IUD or DMPA (injectable) as preferred. If using a progestin-only implant, additional barrier contraception is needed during TB therapy.

A15.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Sections 17.4.1 and 17.4.1.2 (Pulmonary tuberculosis, in adults)

A16.overview: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This entry is used when TB is diagnosed clinically (based on symptoms, chest X-ray, and/or exposure history) without bacteriological confirmation — i.e. the TB-NAAT or smear was not positive, but the clinical picture strongly suggests TB. Treatment follows the same 6-month regimen as confirmed TB (2RHZE/4RH).
phases: Intensive phase (Months 1–2) — RHZE 4-drug combination daily
Continuation phase (Months 3–6) — RH 2-drug combination daily
Completion — clinical resolution at month 6

medications.name: RHZE — Rifampicin + Isoniazid + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (fixed-dose combination)
medications.frequency: Once daily, same time each day
medications.notes: The 4-in-1 tablet contains Rifampicin 150 mg + Isoniazid 75 mg + Pyrazinamide 400 mg + Ethambutol 275 mg. Take all tablets in ONE dose (not divided). May be taken with food to minimise nausea. Rifampicin may turn urine, sweat and tears orange — this is harmless. Rifampicin reduces effectiveness of combined oral contraceptives — advise alternative contraception.

medications.name: RH — Rifampicin + Isoniazid (fixed-dose combination)
medications.frequency: Once daily, same time each day
medications.notes: Two formulations available: RH 150/75 mg and RH 300/150 mg. Depending on weight, either 5 tablets of RH 150/75 OR 2 tablets of RH 300/150 is used. Continue every day without interruption.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.duration: Full duration of TB treatment (6 months)
medications.phase: Adjunct — given with all TB medicines
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy. Routinely given to patients with HIV, malnutrition, or existing neuropathy.

lifestyleAdvice: Take all your TB tablets every day without missing any dose — this is essential for cure
Take all tablets together in ONE dose at the same time each day
You may take tablets with food to reduce nausea
Do not stop treatment even if you feel better — completing 6 months is essential to prevent resistance
If you miss more than 2 doses, tell your CHW or clinic immediately
Cover your mouth when you cough or sneeze — TB spreads through the air
Open windows and let in sunlight at home — TB spreads less in well-ventilated spaces
Sleep in a separate room from others if possible during the first 2 weeks of treatment
Eat a nutritious, balanced diet — TB treatment works best with good nutrition
Stop smoking and avoid excessive alcohol — both worsen TB and slow recovery
Attend every follow-up appointment
Wear a mask in crowded public spaces while you are still infectious (first 2 weeks)
Inform close contacts (family, colleagues) so they can be screened for TB
If you have HIV, take your ART alongside TB treatment every day
Report any of these immediately: yellow eyes/skin, dark urine, severe nausea, tingling in hands/feet, skin rash

everyVisit: Weight — adjust tablet count if weight changes significantly
Ask about adherence — how many doses missed
Ask about side effects (nausea, rash, tingling, yellow eyes)
Check for clinical improvement (cough, fever, weight gain)
baseline: Sputum TB-NAAT — if negative, still treat if clinical picture is convincing
Sputum smear microscopy and culture (for confirmation)
Chest X-ray if available — suggestive findings support diagnosis
HIV test — if positive, refer for ART
Baseline ALT (if jaundiced or risk factors for liver disease)
Screen for diabetes if risk factors

A16.followUpSchedule: Monthly clinical review. Sputum smear microscopy at month 2, month 5, and month 6. If smear remains positive at month 2, consider adherence issues and drug-resistant TB — refer for evaluation. Note: for clinically-diagnosed (unconfirmed) TB, the response to treatment is the main confirmation of the diagnosis.
warningSigns: Yellow eyes or skin (jaundice)
Dark brown urine
Severe nausea or vomiting with abdominal pain
New skin rash — especially with fever, mucosal involvement, or facial swelling
Tingling or numbness in hands or feet
Persistent fever or worsening cough after starting treatment
Coughing up blood (haemoptysis)
Severe chest pain or difficulty breathing
Weight loss despite treatment
referralCriteria: TB meningitis (refer urgently — defer ART for 8 weeks)
Failure to improve after 2 months of treatment despite adherence
Treatment failure (positive smear at month 5 or 6)
Severe adverse drug reactions (hepatitis, drug rash, peripheral neuropathy worsening despite pyridoxine)
TB in children (<12 years) requiring chest X-ray for diagnosis
Contact of a patient with drug-resistant TB
Unable to be managed on an ambulatory basis
Pregnancy — refer for expert TB management

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Signs of disseminated TB, TB meningitis, or severe adverse drug reaction (hepatitis, drug rash with systemic features)
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Refer to hospital same day. For suspected TB meningitis (fever + neck stiffness + headache): urgent LP and referral. For suspected drug-induced hepatitis: STOP all TB medicines before referral.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening if not treated promptly. Do not delay referral.

specialCases.note: Treat TB and HIV. Start TB treatment first, then add ART based on CD4: <50 = within 2 weeks; ≥50 = defer until 8 weeks. Watch for IRIS. Rifampicin reduces DTG concentration — double DTG dose to 50 mg twice daily while on rifampicin.
Ethambutol 15–25 mg/kg three times weekly. Pyrazinamide 20–30 mg/kg three times weekly. Rifampicin and isoniazid do not require dose adjustment.
Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol are all safe in pregnancy. Give pyridoxine 25 mg daily.
Rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide can cause hepatitis. If jaundice or hepatitis symptoms develop: stop all TB medicines, refer urgently for same-day ALT.
Give 25 mg daily alongside TB treatment to prevent isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

Rifampicin reduces the efficacy of combined oral contraceptives and progestin-only implants. Advise IUD or DMPA. If using a progestin-only implant, additional barrier contraception is needed during TB therapy.
